questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A paraphrase that lowers a finding's strength
questions.learningObjective: Explain how hedging language weakens the finding it reports
questions.stem: Marta's log paraphrases a survey finding as: 'The survey suggests that variable stars may sometimes be hard to measure accurately.' Explain what this paraphrase does to the strength of the original finding.

answer.exemplar: The paraphrase weakens the finding at three points. The survey reported a reliable result, but 'suggests' replaces an assertion with a hint, 'may' replaces a definite statement with a possibility, and 'sometimes' replaces a general pattern with an occasional exception. A reader who checks the source would find a firmer claim than the paraphrase conveys.

questions.explanation: Hedged verbs and extra qualifiers reduce the force of a finding without adding information. Each hedge shifts the claim toward 'possible sometimes' rather than 'observed here', so the paraphrase understates its source.
questions.hint: Count the hedges you added to the source's wording.

answer.exemplar: The paraphrase turns a finding into a possibility. questions.stem: In a log about variable stars, Fatima cites a book on stellar lifetimes as support for a claim that observer fatigue causes misidentified variables. Explain what that citation establishes.

answer.exemplar: It establishes almost nothing about the claim. The book's subject is how long stars last and how they evolve; it contains no observation of observers, no protocol for fatigue and no comparison of error rates between tired and rested observers. It is a credible source on a different question, so it can be cited for that question only, and the fatigue claim needs evidence that measures observer error directly.

questions.explanation: A source is relevant only if it reports the thing being claimed. A book on stellar lifetimes may be sound and still say nothing about observer fatigue, so the citation supports no part of the claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that can be tested and one that cannot
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a thesis with unfixed terms cannot be tested
questions.stem: A log records a thesis: 'Telescopes were not important in early modern science.' Explain why this thesis cannot be tested as it stands.

answer.exemplar: The thesis is untestable because its terms are unfixed. 'Important' has no stated measure: it could mean influence on practice, on published results, on funding, or on what later astronomers believed. options.misconception: both weakens the threshold and inflates the effect

options.text: Image contrast is mostly a matter of mirror surface quality
options.misconception: broadens a specific finding into a general rule

questions.explanation: A faithful paraphrase keeps the amount, the effect and the confidence the source used. The others add a possibility, change the threshold, or widen a narrow finding into a general rule.
questions.hint: Keep the threshold and the stated effect.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A source cited for a claim it was not read for
questions.learningObjective: Choose the correct response to an irrelevant cited source
questions.stem: In a bibliography note, Cleo lists a book about telescope history to support a claim about how modern adaptive optics works. What should she do before keeping the citation?

options.text: Keep the citation, since a history of telescopes obviously covers modern instruments
options.misconception: assumes a broad title implies the treatment of the topic

options.text: Keep the citation but describe the book as covering modern techniques
options.misconception: adds a description the source may not warrant

options.text: Move the citation to a general introduction where the claim is not made
options.misconception: hides an irrelevant source where it will not be checked

options.text: Find the passages on adaptive optics and check they support the claim, or drop it

questions.explanation: A citation is a claim about content, so it must be checked against content. If the book does not treat adaptive optics, find a relevant passage or drop the source and replace it.
questions.hint: Read the source on the point you attribute to it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two conventions inside one reference list
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reading difficulty created by two systems in one list
questions.stem: A reference list in a student's astronomy essay mixes a numbered style for journal articles with an author-date style for books. Explain what a reader is asked to do by that list.

answer.exemplar: The reader is asked to decode two systems at once. With author-date entries the reader expects the year beside the author and looks the work up in a bibliography; with numbered entries the reader expects to find the number in the text and match it to a list ordered as the writer chose. Neither convention is wrong, but a reader who meets both cannot scan the list or cite from it without first working out which rule governs which entry.

questions.explanation: A reader scans a reference list by predicting where each detail will sit. Two systems break that expectation, so the reader must work out the rules entry by entry before the list can be used.
questions.hint: Ask how the reader finds an entry's year.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an examination under time pressure requires
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step that converts a plan into a timed answer

stimulus.body: Exam practice, topic: early photochemistry. Timer set for thirty minutes. My plan so far says only: 'write about light and chemistry, use the silver-halide example, and finish with the limits of the claim.' I have not written a thesis.

questions.stem: Looking at this practice log, which step would turn the plan into a timed answer?

options.text: Write the claim the plan's example and limits will support, in one sentence
Research two more examples so the essay has more material to draw on
options.misconception: collects more material before deciding what the essay argues

options.text: Write the conclusion first, so the ending is settled before the body
options.misconception: begins with the end while the claim is still undecided

options.text: Rehearse the introduction aloud to make sure the opening is confident
options.misconception: spends the practice time on delivery rather than on argument

questions.explanation: A plan naming an example and a limit is already shaped like an argument, but the claim joining them is missing. Writing that one sentence first makes every later choice answerable.
questions.hint: Write the load-bearing parts first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an essay plan makes visible
questions.learningObjective: Choose the plan feature that reveals an argument rather than a list
questions.stem: Which feature of an essay plan would tell a writer that the plan's claims form an argument rather than a list?

options.text: The number of sources listed for each of the claims
options.misconception: measures the evidence supply rather than its logical connection

options.text: A stated reason connecting each claim to the one before it
The order in which the observations were actually made
options.misconception: mistakes chronological order for a logical order of reasons

options.text: The length of the conclusion written into the plan
options.misconception: judges the plan by a section's size rather than by its logic

questions.explanation: An argument requires each claim to be connected to the previous one by a reason. A plan that records those connections shows whether the parts support one conclusion or merely sit together.
questions.hint: Look for the reason linking each claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis that can be tested and one that cannot
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a thesis is made testable and what counts against it
questions.stem: Rafiq's thesis reads: 'Observation of the northern sky is more rewarding in winter.' Which change would make this thesis testable, and what would then count against it?

options.text: Keep the thesis, and count against it any winter with poor observing
options.misconception: adds a test that any single unremarkable night could fail

options.text: Keep the thesis, and count against it the opinions of experienced observers
options.misconception: treats opinion as evidence about a claim that records could settle

options.text: Replace it with a claim about measurable conditions, and count contrary records
Keep the thesis but require two people to agree before it can stand
options.misconception: makes truth depend on agreement rather than on evidence

questions.explanation: A thesis about enjoyment cannot be checked against records, since no measurement matches it. Rewriting it as a claim about measurable conditions makes it answerable to contrary evidence.
questions.hint: Reword the claim in terms that can be measured.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Whether a source fits the claim being made
questions.learningObjective: Identify the question that tests whether a source fits a claim
questions.stem: Which question best tests whether a source fits the claim it is offered to support?

options.text: Is the source written by a well-known author in the field
options.misconception: judges fit by reputation rather than by subject matter

options.text: Is the source recent enough to reflect current understanding
options.misconception: judges fit by date rather than by what the claim needs

options.text: Is the source widely cited by other writers on the same topic
options.misconception: judges fit by popularity rather than by evidence

options.text: Does the source report the specific thing the claim asserts

questions.explanation: Fit is a question of subject: a source fits when it reports the thing the claim asserts. Reputation, recency and citation counts describe how a source is received, not whether it carries a claim.
questions.hint: Compare the source's subject with the claim.
